title: The Taproom-Only Brewery Model | Craft Beer School
desc: How a brewery that sells only from its own taproom earns, what it costs to run. It also names the numbers that decide whether the model works.
teaser: No distributor, no retailer margin, no packaging line. A taproom-only brewery keeps the full price and carries the whole venue.
standfirst: A taproom-only brewery sells everything it makes across its own bar. This guide explains the economics, the costs people underestimate and who the model suits.
sections:
A taproom-only brewery brews on site and sells its beer only to people who walk in. Some also sell food and merchandise. Some add takeaway where the rules allow. There is no distributor, no retailer and usually no packaging line beyond growlers or a few kegs.

The appeal is clear. You keep the full selling price, get paid at the till and talk to your customers every day. The weakness is just as clear: your sales cannot exceed the footfall you can attract and serve.
Why the margin looks so good

Each pint carries your price without a trade margin on top. Take the example in the unit economics of a keg, a can and a pint: a pint in your own room earns far more per litre than a keg sold to a bar. Cash is also immediate, which helps with working capital.

But a pint's margin must carry the venue: rent, staff, licence costs, utilities, insurance, cleaning, glass breakage and the hours when nobody comes.
The costs that come with the room

A taproom is a hospitality business. It needs service staff, a licence to sell on premises, safe layout, fire and sanitary approvals, toilets, music and entertainment permissions where required and waste handling. Licensing is a state matter in India and the rules, fees and timings change, so take advice early.

Food is the usual question. Serving food raises the spend per head and the time guests stay, but it adds a kitchen, a food licence and waste. Some taprooms invite visiting food vendors or let guests bring their own, which keeps the model light. Whichever you choose, check the rules in your state, because the combination of food and alcohol service is licensed locally. Location drives everything. A site with steady passing traffic costs more rent, but a cheap site in a quiet lane needs you to create the footfall yourself.

Work backwards from fixed costs. Hypothetical numbers in currency units: monthly fixed costs of 450,000, a net price of 350 per 500 ml pint and a direct cost of 70 per pint including a share of brewing, glassware and wastage. Contribution is 280 per pint. Break-even is 450,000 divided by 280, about 1,610 pints a month, or around 54 pints a day.

Is that realistic? Count real covers, average pints per head and the hours you are open. Most taprooms live on two or three strong days. Take the busiest day in your plan and ask whether the room, the bar and the kitchen can serve that crowd without long waits. A taproom that cannot serve its peak loses sales it has already earned. Then take the slowest day and ask how many staff you really need. See brewery break-even for the full method.

Your sales ceiling is the number of seats, the opening hours and how long guests stay. If the taproom is full on Saturday and empty on Tuesday, adding tanks does not help. Better use of the quiet hours does: a quiz night, a food partner, a private booking, a tasting.

That pressure also affects the beer. A small range, brewed often and served fresh, suits a taproom. A long list ties up fermenters and wastes beer.

It suits owners who like hospitality, have a good location and want to build a local community. It suits a first brewery where cash is tight. It does not suit those who want to scale beyond one site without another venue or a packaged product. Many taproom breweries later add kegs or cans once the brand is known, which is a separate decision covered in distribution models.

Many taprooms also use the quiet hours for brewery tours or short tasting sessions with a limited number of guests, which brings in visitors without needing extra tanks. Keep the numbers honest: a tour that fills a table on a slow Tuesday is worth more than one that draws the same crowd that would have come on Saturday anyway.

Responsible service matters too. Train staff to refuse service to anyone underage or visibly intoxicated, offer good non-alcoholic options and never promote heavy drinking.
faqs: Is a taproom-only brewery more profitable than selling through distributors?
Often the margin per litre is higher, but the fixed cost of the venue is larger. Compare full contribution after venue costs.
Do I need a food licence as well?
If you serve food, yes. Requirements differ by state and by country. Check with the relevant authorities.
Can I sell takeaway beer from my taproom?
That depends on your licence and the local rules, which differ and change. Ask a licensing adviser.
How many seats do I need?
Work back from the pints per day you need to break even and how long guests stay. Seats follow from that.
